utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: While the witness is coming in, I can deal with certain matters. We will sit from now until 4.00 today. We'll have a half-hour break at that stage, 4.00 till 4.30, and then we'll sit from 4.30 to 5.45 and break for 20 minutes at that stage. Secondly, Judge Chowhan is unfortunately unwell, we've had to consider the situation in light of that, but considering in view of the stage we've reached with this witness and case in the case in general and other developments this week and looking at the evidence that is likely to be heard in his absence, we consider it is in the interests of justice to continue in his absence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thirdly, Mr. Zecevic, there is an application for the admission of exhibits from the bar table filed on the 16th of August and a supplementary application filed on the 23rd of August. We wish you to try to provide further information in relation to certain of these items, and rather than do it formally through a written order we'll extend that request to you here and hope that you did can comply with it. There are a number of press releases which are 1D598 and 599, 605, 607, 608, and 609. We would invite you to try to provide further information as to the authenticity, including the source, of these documents. There is a BBC press release which appears to have been obtained by them from Tanjug, and therefore it's second-hand even on the face of it. It's 1D690 and we would like you to provide further information, if possible, as to the authenticity of that document, including its source.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And finally, there are a number of documents -- I think they're all decisions -- no, mostly decisions, but also enactments which fall under 1D638. We would invite you to explain what issues in the trial these documents are relevant to and their significance.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Hopefully you can do that by Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'll find out in a moment whether there is any more cross-examination for you, but whatever is asked of you today, please bear in mind that the solemn declaration you made at the beginning continues to apply to your evidence right to the end. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Just briefly, Your Honour, a few more questions, with your leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Good afternoon, General.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I would like you to have a quick look at the document we have labelled here P1459. Can you look at the first page of it you'll see that it's a strictly confidential memo from the 3rd Corps forward command post to the chief of the command staff of the 25th of May, 1999. Look at paragraph 3 of the document. We'll get to the second page later, but I can tell you that this is a document that is signed by the commander of the 3rd Corps, General Pavkovic. But if you look at paragraph 3 for the time being, he's saying that "MUP members condoned or openly permit evident criminal activities and plunder committed by their fellow MUP members as well as civilians resulting in the misappropriation of a vast number of motor vehicles, technical goods, and other resources from the territory of Kosovo."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And if we could turn over to paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You see here accusing the MUP of committing serious crimes against the Albanian civilian population the refugee shelters referred to as murder, rape, et cetera. And I'd like you before I ask you a couple of questions also to read the concluding paragraph, there's a paragraph below paragraph 7?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The proposed measures, is that what you mean? "In light of the above said," that's how it begins.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, please read it to yourself.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Were you aware, General, that the leadership of the 3rd Corps was making these allegations about the MUP conducting Kosovo, that is they were committing looting on a large scale as well as even more serious crimes, like murder, rape, plunder, and aggravated robbery, were you aware of these allegations against the MUP?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this is the first time that I see this document in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, you see in the measures proposed a recommendation that the MUP be subordinated to the Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that I did say yesterday. I did talk yesterday about this so-called ...

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the question is not the question, it's the interpretation. It doesn't say -- or translation. It doesn't say anywhere in the text that the Ministry of the Interior should be subordinated to the Joint Command. The word "subordinate" does not read in the original --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, if you feel that your position has been prejudiced by this cross-examination, we will allow you to further cross-examine the witness to clarify any point of that nature. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that's not what I meant. I said that there has been a misinterpretation from English into Serbian, not the question. I'm not opposed to the question itself. What is written here is not what we got in our earphones, so perhaps if my learned friend could read it the way it is written. That's my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just give me a second until I see that. There's no question, Mr. Fila, of the text being mistranslated. What we have in English is what Mr. Stamp actually said. Now, Mr. Stamp, do you think that this ought to be rephrased or do you intend --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I could just save time if I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Were you aware of recommendations from the 3rd command leadership that the MUP should be placed under command of what is called the Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think you said in your statement or in evidence yesterday that you were privy to all if not most of the documents that were sent to the Supreme Command Staff because you were a member of the staff. Had you ever seen any document emanating from the 3rd command or the Pristina Corps referring to the Joint Command in the course of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. If I may make a remark, this document is addressed to the chief of the Supreme Command Staff, but it does not have a reference number of any sort. It has not been entered into any records, which is an obligation. This must be done in accordance with the protocol.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, there are reference numbers it seems to me, and you probably could tell me, on the first page. Strictly confidential number 872-94/1-2.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If you could return to the first page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this is the reference number from the place where the document originated from, but it was not entered into any records or filed at the place where it was addressed to. And I have never seen this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we move on quickly to P1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And these are minutes of a meeting of the MUP staff for Kosovo and Metohija of the 7th of May, 1999, that is just a few days before the date of the last document you saw. And you see that this meeting that Mr. Nikola Sainovic took part in the meeting, and it was chaired by Major-General Lukic of the MUP. I'd like to take you to page 5 of that document, and that's page 4 in B/C/S. The relevant part reading - and I'm not sure if you're able to see all of the B/C/S, the left margin might be --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it quite well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: On the previous page it is indicated that this is the chief of the SUP in Pristina at the secretariat for internal affairs in Pristina, Colonel Bogoljub Janicevic speaking. And he is saying "There are many problems in connection active duty and reserve VJ soldiers. They drive around in vehicles without license plates and have items whose origins are unknown. A large number of vehicles have not been registered, and they are marked with stickers. Every other VJ officer has been observed driving a civilian vehicle with such markings. The military has not taken sufficient measures and most crimes are being perpetrated by VJ members. VJ volunteer units and VJ uniforms must be disbanded. VJ members and vehicles refuse to stop at check-points, drive away from the police, and when they do stop, threaten the police with their weapons to pass without being checked." This is the report of the chief of the MUP for Pristina. If we go further on in this document to page 9 in English, which is page 7 in B/C/S, and it's not indicated on the page that I've mentioned, so -- but I will quote what is indicated on the previous page, that this is a report of a chief of a SUP in Urosevac, Colonel Bozidar Filic, and he reported: "Our relations with the VJ are the same as those of other SUPs. VJ officers behave rather incomprehensibly, and when a soldier is handed over to them for looting they set him free with the excuse that'these are our men." Were you aware in May, that is, before the meetings with President Milosevic, that the MUP or the leadership of the MUP in Kosovo were claiming that the VJ officers were committing crimes in Kosovo with impunity, that the VJ organisation was not doing anything or sufficient to prevent them from committing these crimes?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not known to me, this is the first time I hear of this, and at this meeting with Milosevic, this was not discussed, that's point number one. Secondly, as far as I can see, this mostly deals with the theft of cars and this was punished in a number of ways by military courts quite vigorously. But this is not something that I knew of and this was not discussed at the meeting with the then-President Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said that after the meeting with President Milosevic one of the decisions was that there would be a meeting with the leadership of the DB --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- what was that meeting intended to cover? What was supposed to be the subject of that meeting?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the subject was supposed to be the same subject that was discussed at a meeting with the then-President Milosevic. The crimes and other acts that are in contravention of the international law of war, and agreement about joint efforts that would resolve all those problems as soon as possible and within the legal framework and also some relations between various people, how these could be improved and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you said the DB avoided attending that meeting or did not attend that meeting?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean at Milosevic's?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The meeting that was arranged between the leadership of the army and the DB, the DB failed to attend.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was not to be a meeting between the military leadership and the state security, but the state security and the security administration leaders. And on the 18th, the day after the meeting with Mr. Milosevic, we made all the preparations for this meeting, but it was not organised at the end because the state security did not prove to be quite cooperative in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: As head or as a senior member of the security administration in the VJ with security organs in Kosovo, I wish to ask you again: Do you know what the various units that were attached to the MUP in Kosovo, like the Arkanovci and the Drina Wolves, were doing in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, this has been asked and answered ad nauseam.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think I asked him once, and I admit that he did say no. He did not know. But he has seen quite a few documents since then, and I just wish, having regard to all of that, if he could be given another opportunity to comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let's see whether the lapse of time makes any difference. Please ask the question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you still maintain, sir, to this Court, that you in your capacity did not know what the Drina Wolves and the Arkanovci were doing in Kosovo during the conflict?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you what I knew regarding Arkan and his men, that they had killed two civilians. And two or three days later at a meeting, this was confirmed by Rade Markovic that this information was accurate, that they were arrested --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic, we don't want to hear again what you've told us. Mr. Stamp wants to know what additional information you can give him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, I can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours. I have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic, I'd like to ask you a number of questions about one matter. What in March 1999 did you understand by the term "Supreme Command"?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did the presidents of Serbia and Montenegro have any part to play in the Supreme Command?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were the Supreme Defence Council. It was a body that made decisions related to the defence of the country and also the preparation and the use of the Army of Yugoslavia as part of that; and pursuant to their decisions, the Commander-in-Chief made his own decisions, issued his orders, and so on. And on the basis of that, the chief of the Supreme Command Staff, in accordance with Article 5 of the Law on the Army of Yugoslavia, is the highest staff and expert organ for the use and preparation of the Army of Yugoslavia; he then in turn issued appropriate orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does that mean that you understand the Supreme Command to have existed prior to March 1999 also?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the Supreme Defence Council did exist, the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia existed, and the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia; that's what existed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I ask that question because the translation of your last answer said: "On the basis of that," that's the decisions of the Supreme Defence Council, "the chief of the Supreme Command Staff in accordance with Article 5 of the Law on the Army of ... is the highest staff and expert organ for the use and preparation of the Army of Yugoslavia ..."

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The interpreter may have missed something. The Supreme Defence Council makes decisions pursuant to those decisions, the Commander-in-Chief makes his own decisions, issues orders related to the preparation and use of the army, and the Chief of the General Staff or of the Supreme Command Staff, and I don't want to repeat everything what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When the Commander-in-Chief was making decisions during the war, that's from and after the 24th of March, did you understand him to be acting pursuant to decisions of the Supreme Defence Council?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you able to identify what decisions of the Supreme Defence Council he would be acting pursuant to in conducting the war?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: State of war was declared and the state of war implies the undertaking of all measures which -- well, it means that the army moves into a state of war, mobilisation, certain decisions are made there, the Supreme Defence Council and so on -- but I couldn't really say specifically. I don't know what the Supreme Defence Council did; I didn't attend their meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You were never at a meeting of the Supreme Defence Council?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But you did attend meetings of the Supreme Command Staff.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As part of the security administration, I was a member of the Supreme Command Staff, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And were you also in that position a member of the General Staff of the VJ prior to the 24th of March?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the date that you mentioned, the chief of the security administration, then General Aleksandar Dimitrijevic, was a member of the VJ General Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you aware that in addition to the president of the federal republic, that the Supreme Command consisted of other people connected with the army?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but could you be a bit more specific, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was your understanding that the chief of the staff that would by then be the chief of the Supreme Command Staff was also a member of the Supreme Command?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I explained that when you asked me what the Supreme Command consisted of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Were you aware of any ministers of the government, other than the president of the federal republic, being a member of the Supreme Command?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. From what I know, they could have been summoned to some meetings if their department was involved and it was of interest for the defence of the country, but they were not officially members of the Supreme Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's a different question. My question relates to the presence of the involvement of ministers of the government in the Supreme Command, that's when the war started and thereafter.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In the meetings that you attended when the war was ongoing, were decisions made that involved the president as the supreme commander and others there contributing to these decisions?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Reports were sent to the president, daily reports, relating to the events in the area not only of Kosovo but in the area of Yugoslavia, relating to the NATO bombing. As for the -- this is in relation to the Supreme Command Staff. As for the rest, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I appreciate the nature of the meetings you were holding on the 16th and 17th of May, and it's not these that I'm now going to talk about. Between the 24th of March and the beginning of May, did you attend any other meetings at which the president of the federal republic was present?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, do you wish to ask anything further?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I must put questions that arose from the cross-examination of Mr. Stamp. I actually didn't have any questions for the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Gajic, we will be going fast if you answer with a answer.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: As regards the Joint Command I'm going to tell you something else. Witnesses were heard by the Sainovic Defence here, first of all, Momir Bulatovic, who in his testimony on page 13817 and on, stated that he made the decision to send the vice-president of the federal government to Kosovo, Nikola Sainovic, who was in charge of foreign policy, because at the time there were many foreigners in Kosovo, which you confirmed, and so on and so forth. The same thing was stated by Zivadin Jovanovic, foreign minister, as well as the three persons you mentioned, Minic, Matkovic, Andjelkovic, then Andreja Milosavljevic and all of those who were involved in the defence confirmed that Momir Bulatovic and the government of Yugoslavia sent Nikola Sainovic to Kosovo. Yesterday you said that General Dimitrijevic told you that he was sent by Slobodan Milosevic. Do you allow for the possibility that General Dimitrijevic was mistaken and that Nikola Sainovic was actually sent by the Government of Yugoslavia, just like the prime minister said and all of those from the government?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I allow for that possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The next thing I would like to ask you is the following. You explained the nature of the meetings of the Joint Command as the army referred to it. In order to understand properly what we're talking about here, the question is what the Joint Command means, not whether that that name was used. I used -- I accept that it was used by the army, but what I'm interested in is what it means. You explained the nature of the meetings, and you said that this was more for the purposes of coordination. Mr. Gajic, you as a senior officer, lower or higher ranking, in your view, this Joint Command that included these four members, four civilians, ordered the army, the use of troops, reactions, execution of tasks, and so on, or was it more likely, as testified here before this Tribunal by Minic, Matkovic, and Andjelkovic, that these were meetings where information was exchanged about the military, police, politics, the economy, and not that plans of action and attacks were reviewed?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with you. In these meetings that you are talking about it was demonstrated that there was no interference in command or in relation to the command of the Pristina Corps or the MUP staff which was headed by General Sreten Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. In preparation for this testimony you looked at all of the collegium minutes of the Main Staff of the VJ. Did you find anywhere that anyone, Aca Dimitrijevic and others, mentioned a Joint Command that was commanding the troops of the VJ in Kosovo, did you see anything like that anywhere?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not and I explained that I think yesterday or the day before.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. You toured the units and the security organs in Kosovo and Metohija in 1999 in June together with General Aleksandar Vasiljevic. Did any of the security staff at any level mention to you that in the Pristina Corps or the 3rd Army anywhere civilian command was interfering and deploying the troops?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did not mention anything like that, and I did not meet any of the civilians who were there. I went to Kosovo six times in the course of 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I'm speaking about 1999.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I went there in 1999, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Would you then accept that units of the Army of Yugoslavia as well as the security organs in Kosovo and Metohija were used exclusively within orders which they received by the superior commands in 1999 and on.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that command or chain of command was the one that was functioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment, in case you want to ask anything as the result of this. Mr. Gajic, yesterday you told us the source of your information about the Joint Command was Mr. Dimitrijevic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said specifically that the first information, not about the Joint Command, but about sending Mr. Sainovic and Mr. Minic to Kosovo for coordination, and I said that this was about political and economic questions, as well as coordination in relation to the army and the MUP. This is my information. At the time or later he did not mention any Joint Command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Am I wrong in thinking that he was the source of your information, or did you have information about the Joint Command from another source?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first information came from him - I said that yesterday - this was in late June or early July. And later the so-called Joint Command name appeared and started to circulate and that I heard about later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Perhaps my question could be more precise. Is he the sole source of your information about what it was the Joint Command were doing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I explained that yesterday, that we in the Supreme Command Staff, when the aggression of the 24th of March began, that we did not receive a single document from the so-called Joint Command, neither did the Supreme Command Staff send such a document -- any document to the Joint Command. We did not discuss or mention the Joint Command. The line was the Supreme Command Staff, the 3rd Army staff, and the Pristina Corps staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to take that as a yes. You have to bear in mind that we have seen other documents that you plainly haven't seen in relation to the Joint Command. And I just wanted to know if there was any other person or source of information had told you what it was the Joint Command were actually doing, and I think you're saying there was no such source; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you be a little more specific, please, and since you're putting that question probably I allow for the possibility that you do have some other sources in mind. I will answer, but I just need more details, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm trying to understand what appears to me to be a conflict between what you said yesterday and what you're saying today, because yesterday you said that you were told that -- first of all, that it was Milosevic that sent Sainovic; and secondly, that he was to coordinate activities between the VJ and the MUP in the struggle against terrorism. And now you're saying it might not have been Milosevic but Bulatovic, without any basis for indicating to us you think it might be Bulatovic. And you're also saying that coordination didn't mean interfering in any way with the command of the VJ and the MUP. Now, I want to know what other sources you have for giving these further explanations, that's all, to understand the difference between today and yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First, allow me to explain that in response to Mr. Fila's question, I said that it was possible. Mr. Sainovic was federal Deputy Prime minister, and Momir Bulatovic was Prime minister. I said it was possible that federal prime-minister sent his deputy prime-minister. And second, that does not rule out Mr. Milosevic, because federal Prime minister definitely informed, and received some consent from, the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. So these two things are not in collision. But what I said about coordination -- and I said this had to do with political and economic problems, coordination on those issues, as well as coordination between the MUP and the army in the fight against terrorism, and I stand by my statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Evidently there's a problem in -- Mr. Gajic, if I understood you correctly today, General Dimitrijevic never mentioned the Joint Command to you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I think that we understand each other. Yesterday, today, you never said that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So Mr. Dimitrijevic, General Dimitrijevic, told you that -- he informed you that Slobodan Milosevic sent Sainovic and Minic to Kosovo for coordination?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And he didn't even mention Matkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Minic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did not mention Matkovic or Andjelkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So Mr. Aleksandar Dimitrijevic never mentioned to you or to the General Staff the words "Joint Command"?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: All right. So that's done. Let's continue. When Minic, Matkovic, and Andjelkovic testified here, an exhibit by the Prosecution was read out at P1012, and if you can believe me - you know I'm not lying - it's a decision of the Main Board of the SPS chaired by Slobodan Milosevic - and I agree with you that it could not have been without him - and the SPS on its Main Board decides that it was sending a Working Group headed by Milomir Minic, an SPS Working Group, comprising Milomir Minic, Bakija Andjelkovic, and Dusan Matkovic. This is what it says in this document which you can see if you wish, now you will see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 4 of this document, can we show that to the witness, paragraph 4, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: From this document you can see that these three were sent by the Main Board of the SPS, and if you look at that you will see it, paragraph 1. Can you please read that to yourself, item 1, and there you can see who is sending them to Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I wasn't aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. So we can infer based on this that the SPS Main Board sent this delegation of three, this Working Group, to Kosovo and not Slobodan Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what the document says.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: To be entirely fair to you and to Mr. Fila, Mr. Gajic, let me read your answer yesterday on the Joint Command. The question was: "What was the Joint Command, to your knowledge?" And your answer then was: "That was a type of coordinating body. My first information about that is some coordination, and the information came at the end of June or beginning of July 1998. This information was conveyed to me by General Dimitrijevic, the then-head of the security administration." Now, that's your answer to a question about what was the Joint Command, and you tell us where you learned about it apparently. Now you say that Dimitrijevic did not tell you about it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Dimitrijevic did not mention the Joint Command. He mentioned -- I mean --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He did not use the term "Joint Command." He talked about sending people for the purposes of coordination over there, and that is a different matter altogether.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- so where did you learn of the Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While preparing for this testimony, I learned about something called the Joint Command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In what context did you learn of it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Something to the effect that there was something called a Joint Command which like -- had to do with the involvement of the army's units and the MUP units in the struggle against terrorism.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And this is knowledge that you claim you have acquired in preparation for giving evidence here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So when you've been asked questions throughout your evidence about your knowledge, is it possible that you're speaking about what you've known simply by reading the papers or hearing about them in preparation to give evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I remember, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So we can't rely on your evidence as being your own personal recollection of events; it may be something you've constructed from the proofing process that you've gone through with counsel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not accept that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Just to wrap this up, in 1999 you were up there or down there in Kosovo. Did you and General Aleksandar Vasiljevic at any point write any sort of report or inform the Main Staff, the Supreme Command, whoever you like, about disruption to the command system of units and interference by a body called the Joint Command or whatever else we might yet come up with by the end of this trial?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we wrote no report but there is something that happened that I had completely forgotten to mention. General Vasiljevic was at a meeting over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [No interpretation] --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This wraps up the issue of about the Joint Command, as far as I'm concerned, Your Honours, and I'm about to move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic, General --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: One final question on this. You say that you learned about Joint Command in preparation for this trial. How did you learn it? Who did you learn it from or what did you learn it from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know specifically what the circumstances were right now, but I probably looked at those documents and there was probably some sort of a reference to the Joint Command somewhere in those documents, but I really can't be more specific than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So it wasn't a big enough surprise for you to remember where you first found out about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I mean, the first information I got was from General Dimitrijevic, and I think that was a realistic explanation, too, and that's what I took it to be. I believe that this was some sort of coordination because a command is something else and a staff is something else. And I know that according to all the regulations that applied and along any chain of command there was no such thing as envisaged as a Joint Command. Now, why was this termed Joint Command? I really don't know how this came about. It was probably somebody -- I'm not sure who christened it, as people say where I come from, but I don't know what the circumstances were surrounding the name of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would I be wrong in thinking that an army officer in your position hearing of or reading the expression "Joint Command" associated with the VJ and the MUP might have been extremely surprised to have had no prior knowledge of it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You know, I'll answer in a very specific way. I'm a counter-intelligence officer. I was into counter-intelligence business. The line down to my subordinate security bodies was functioning in keeping with all the rules also as concerned relations between me and as superior and them as subordinates. Therefore, I think someone better placed than me to know this could probably answer this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You see, we've heard of a commission for cooperation with the KVM, we've heard of an inter-departmental committee dealing with counter-terrorism, but none of these bodies contained the word "command" and yet they do coordination jobs. And that's what's concerning us is that soldiers like you can read the word "command" and not suddenly be alerted and caused to wonder and inquire what on earth was this. But you just, when you saw it, passed it over as some sort of coordination body.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, and we at the Supreme Command Staff didn't, or rather, did have a prescribed line down to our subordinates, specifically the 3rd Army and the Pristina Corps command. We had no communication and not a single document was exchanged between us and this so-called Joint Command, nor did a single representative of this so-called Joint Command ever turn up at the Supreme Command Staff, never at all. We had no communication at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yesterday in answer to a question by Mr. Stamp, page 18 of yesterday's transcript, you said that once the meeting was over General Ojdanic then spoke to the supreme commander Milosevic, and so on and so forth. It was based on this that I wanted to ask you something. One of the allegations that I read in the indictment, that I had the honour to read in the indictment, is this: Nikola Sainovic commanded General Ojdanic, General Ojdanic stood to attention and saluted him, practically shaking with fear. That was as the war was still ongoing. You as a general, try to imagine this situation. One of the five deputy prime ministers exercising command over Ojdanic and other lower-ranking officers. Do you find that to be an imaginable situation --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Indiscernible] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can we have a reference to the indictment passage, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The indictment claims that he was General Ojdanic's superior --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a reference to commanding Ojdanic, Ojdanic standing to attention, saluting him, and practically shaking with fear, which is the basis -- which is the question you've just put to the witness. And, you know, all counsel here are very anxious to ensure that no misrepresentations are made to witnesses before they're invited to answer a question. So we would like to see the basis for that question in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paragraph 48 of the indictment reads: On a de facto basis, Nikola Sainovic also exercised authority over Dragoljub Ojdanic and their subordinates on instruction from Slobodan Milosevic. To exercise authority over someone who is not mentally ill means to command someone and this includes his subordinates, too, and one of them was Mr. Gajic, which would suggest that Nikola Sainovic also had powers over Nikola [as interpreted] Gajic. And there's another reference about it being saluted in the military way, receiving a military salute, and that is the basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, you've read a passage which talks about command authority and/or effective control over VJ units deployed to Kosovo, including the 3rd Army. Now, that does not state command over the General Staff -- the Supreme Command General Staff that was headed by Mr. Ojdanic. So where is the basis for saying that he was in command over Ojdanic? Never mind all the other silly things about saluting. Let's get the basics. Where is the --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll read this for you. Would you please allow me to reed this for you. It says: "Exercised authority over Dragoljub Ojdanic and their subordinates." Dragoljub Ojdanic is the highest-ranking officer of the VJ. Any of those below him are his subordinates. To exercise authority over someone in Serbian means to be that person's commanders, or if that person is mentally unfit, then you take care of him. And that is the way in which we use the word. In the other text there is an even stronger expression to the same effect in terms of this military salute. So that was my foundation for asking this question, and if I may, Your Honour, I can even rephrase the question, and I'll ask him this. Did Mr. Sainovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a second. You will have to rephrase it. But I accept your explanation now that that sentence is a foundation for your question about commanding Ojdanic on a de facto basis. And you should put these questions in accordance with the terminology of the indictment if it's the indictment you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'll do just that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You heard what I just read, Witness, didn't you? The Prosecutor claims and it reads that Nikola Sainovic, a civilian, exercised authority, exercised authority, over General Dragoljub Ojdanic and his subordinates. That is what it says in no uncertain terms. Is this something that is conceivable for you that anything like this might have happened?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, by no means.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: All right. My next question. Why did I remind you of yesterday's testimony? You say that the communication was normal between the supreme commander and the Chief of the General Staff, as it should have been. All the -- under the chain of command, right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Is there any merit at all to the allegation that between the supreme commander and the next man in the chain of command just under him, Dragoljub Ojdanic, there should be interposed Nikola Sainovic and that it was through Nikola Sainovic that Milosevic exercised authority or exercised command --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's a matter -- don't answer that question. That's a matter for the Tribunal to determine.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now please have 3D728, it's a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And you answered a number of questions from Mr. Stamp about that exhibit yesterday. It's the last bit that you couldn't remember when Mr. Ojdanic or whoever said something, or rather --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 3 in the Serbian, the last portion, where there's a reference to adjutant Sreten and Lieutenant-Colonel --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Second lieutenant Sainovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In order to avoid any misinterpretation of what you said yesterday, first of all, the meeting at which this takes place - and you don't remember that - you are at that meeting, aren't you? This is a briefing, right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is a briefing.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: At this briefing -- at this briefing -- at this briefing do we see second lieutenant Sainovic present at the --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That is not the translation -- or that's not the language that the witness used yesterday for that passage. It is the English translation --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is something else that I'm trying to establish, something entirely different. It is not clear who is attending this briefing; that is what I'm trying to put across. Nikola Sainovic is not there, he's not at the briefing, although there's a reference here to an adjutant Sreten and this PPR, it's a simple second lieutenant, but there was a mistranslation.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And secondly, do you know anything at all about this meeting that was allegedly supposed to take place the next day at 9.00 --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The evidence was that the witness in looking at the Cyrillic document interpreted the abbreviations to be Vice-President Sainovic. And I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't dispute that --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't dispute that. I'm just smiling because "PPR" means lieutenant colonel, but it could be an abbreviation used for deputy president, too, it would be illogical of you to claim that those people there were generals because the abbreviation there implies a much lower thank. That's all I'm trying to say. And what about the adjutant, there is no such thing, right --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The note I have of yesterday's evidence is that this was a group to look at matters arising from this meeting; it wasn't a reflection of the people present at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I asked this just in case.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: My second question is whether you, General, know if this meeting was held at all -- if this meeting was held at all and who attended it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's all I had, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May I, with your leave just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, do you have anything arising?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Just a couple questions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, in relation to matters arising from that further cross-examination, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Fila said that you had read all of the Joint Command -- sorry, all of the collegium minutes in preparation for your testimony, is that true, that you read all of the collegium minutes?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I -- I think that I looked at most of those things that were of interest for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But -- well, you are not really answering my question. The question is: Did you read all of the collegium minutes -- do you know if read all of the collegium minutes or you read what was given to you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please give me a time-frame. Minutes from what time-period, if you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you read the collegium minutes for the 18th of March, 1999?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That's P938. You said that you never saw any reference to the Joint Command in the collegium minutes. Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My evidence is that I did not hear of that word.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, to be precise, I think Mr. Fila said in a question to you or put it to you that you did not see the reference, any reference, to the Joint Command when you reviewed the collegium minutes, and you did not answer him directly. So I'm asking you directly: When you reviewed the joint -- not the Joint Command minutes, the collegium minutes, for the 18th of March in 1999, did you not see any reference to the Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible that it was mentioned in one or two places, but I don't know whether it was on the 18th of March because I don't remember that date. But I did get the information, and I had already formed my opinion of that. I knew what it was all about, that it was some kind of a coordination thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And as to why this term was used, why this name was coined, who did it, why this term was used, the "Joint Command," I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, two things. First of all, I asked about General Dimitrijevic, whether General Dimitrijevic had ever told him about the Joint Command and whether General Dimitrijevic used that term, that was my question, and he said no. And I would like the Prosecutor to have the document called up on the screen when a reference is made to it because I would like to look at it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, can you tell me where I find the question about reading all the collegium minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is at -- question by Mr. Fila: "In preparation for your testimony, you looked at all of the collegium" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please speak in the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm so sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you give me the page and line.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Page 15, line 6 following. Mr. Fila asked: "In preparation for your testimony, you looked at all of the collegium minutes of the Main Staff of the VJ. Did you find anywhere that anyone Aca Dimitrijevic or others mentioned a Joint Command that was commanding the troops of the VJ in Kosovo, did you see anything like that anywhere?" And the witness said: "No, I did not, and I explained that" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you've got that much now clear. Did you have any further question?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, but I do have an objection. Your Honour, General Aleksandar Dimitrijevic in this time-period was not a member of the collegium on the 18th of March -- oh, I do apologise, he was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And the lack of dates is, of course, in your question. It's a -- you were unspecific in the question, so Mr. Stamp is perfectly entitled --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- to ask the question the way he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, I am not objecting, but I just want him to show the page because he's saying that -- actually what it says on this page is "collegium." I want him to pin-point where the word "Joint Command" is actually mentioned, where the words "Joint Command" are mentioned in P938. That's what I want him to do. I'm not saying that no mention is made; I just want him to pin-point where it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're not required to display it for that purpose, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Counsel have access to these documents if they want to study them individually as we proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Just -- you don't recall --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May I just ask one last question, Your Honour? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you recall seeing in any of these Joint Command -- any of those collegium minutes that you reviewed, both General Dimitrijevic and also General Ojdanic referring to the Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible. I cannot rule out that possibility. This material is so voluminous that it may have slipped past me. I doubt it but it's possible. But in light of the fact that I had received information and that I had formed my opinion about that, I didn't really pay much attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Just for the record, may I just indicate that I'm referring to P939, page 45 -- sorry, P939, pages 26 to 27.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I have to get up. The document that you displayed is dated March 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: General, do you still maintain --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I have a question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're not entitled just to jump in like that. I didn't even realise --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm asking you for your permission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I didn't even realise that Mr. Stamp had finished. I didn't realise that he had sat down because I was looking in your direction. You're now complete?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Fila, you want to bat the ball back again. What is the basis for asking a further question?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very simple, Your Honour. When asked by this very same gentleman, Mr. Stamp, General Gajic said yesterday what had been called the Joint Command with the members, whoever they were, that it ceased to exist in October 1998. And the document that Mr. Stamp is showing him is dated 1999. If you're asking me to read the indictment in order to find out, what basis is there for him to be showing the documents from 1999? Because I asked questions about 1998. This is when all of this was happening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The simple answer to your question to me is this: You in a question to the witness told him that he had read all the collegium minutes. Now, that covers 1997, 1998, and 1999. Mr. Stamp then -- and you also led from of him that there was no reference by Dimitrijevic or anyone else of the Joint Command. Mr. Stamp is simply putting to the witness a document which falls within the compass of the documents you asked questions about that he maintains contains that reference. These are matters for argument in due course. Mr. Gajic gave very clear evidence yesterday about when the Joint Command operation ceased, but that's a separate question from whether at a later date the Joint Command was being referred to by people in the know. Thank you. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, before I start with my re-examination I would just like to inform you that in the collegium minutes of the 18th of March referenced by my colleague, Mr. Stamp, there is no reference made to the Joint Command. And out of 1.000 pages of the collegium minutes it is mentioned once or twice in just a couple of lines. And I think that this second reference provided by Mr. Stamp is correct, but on the 18th of March no mention is made of the Joint Command, I'm sure of that. I didn't want to intervene, but you can take my word for it. It's 100 per cent accurate, as Mr. Fila would say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, please continue with your re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, yesterday in the cross-examination when Mr. Stamp asked you about the documenting of the meetings of the General Staff, you said that as far as the briefings at the Supreme Command Staff, all of those were recorded and there is the unabridged version of the notes of all the members of the Supreme Command Staff. And then the next question is where the tapes were, and your answer was that they were probably somewhere in the army archives. We all know that the General Staff collegium meetings were recorded and the transcripts were made, the very same transcripts that were used by Mr. Stamp. I want to ask you: During the war, could you think back to that period and could you recall where the meetings of the Supreme Command Staff were held. Do you remember that room?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me whether in that room there was the equipment in place to record the evening briefings that were held at the Supreme Command Staff, if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was no equipment there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Do you allow then that yesterday when you were answering questions asked of you by Mr. Stamp that you made a mistake when you said that all the meetings of the Supreme Command Staff were recorded and that those recordings were in the archives?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was imprecise because this referred to the time before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My second question has to do with a topic related to the so-called arming of Serb civilians. Mr. Stamp asked you - I'll paraphrase - we have information we got from General Samardzic, the 3rd Army commander, or rather, the question was: "In 1998 did -- was the army involved in arming over 40.000 Serb civilians in Kosovo?" Your answer was: "We have information we got from General Samardzic, who was the 3rd Army commander, that this figure was correct, that this is the number of civilians who had weapons, but I will explain why." And then Mr. Stamp asks another question, the figure now is 47.000 - I apologise to the interpreters - and you say: "I think that the figure that you just mentioned," you're referring to Mr. Stamp, "is more or less accurate." Now, my question is not about the figure, who's accuracy you confirmed to Mr. Stamp. What I'm asking you is: To your knowledge, to whom were weapons distributed when we're talking about 40 to 47.000 people? Mr. Stamp put it to you that those were civilians. Could you please explain to the Judges who were these people that the weapons were distributed to?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were civilians, but they were conscripts. They were part of the civilian defence, civilian protection, they were under the jurisdiction of the federal Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Just go slow, General, because of the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Just one more question. These people you said they were members of the civilian defence or civilian protection, were these people part of the system, defence system, so those were not the people who were outside of the system?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not outside of the system. They were under the jurisdiction and authority of the federal defence ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: My next question: Towards the end, again Mr. Stamp put it to you - this is with regard to the orders that you called preventive orders -- well, I'm not going to quote what he's saying, but he is putting to you that all those orders were issued after the crimes against the Kosovo Albanians and the expulsion of the Kosovo Albanians had already been committed. He is putting this to you, and you -- your answer is: "I know that." What I'm asking you now, General: At the time when the orders on the compliance with the humanitarian law or the prevention of crimes and so on, any of those orders that you called preventive orders, did you have any knowledge at that time that any of the crimes alleged in the indictment had been committed?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: What did you -- what was your opinion, General? Why were the Kosovo Albanians leaving the country at the time?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That it was part of an organised system in order to create a situation that was later on labelled a humanitarian catastrophe, and also to facilitate the infiltration of the military factor from the outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't have any questions for this witness. Further questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Clarification again, Mr. Gajic, of what I've noted from yesterday's evidence in relation to the weapons that were given to Serb civilians. My understanding of what you said yesterday was that the VJ opposed this. Is that an accurate understanding?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, perhaps I was imprecise there, but I think that I just gave an explanation now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So in fact the army actually provided the arms; is that the position?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I said about the forming of the civilian defence and the civilian protection units is pursuant to Article 61 of the Law on Defence, and that warehouse. Well, this is under the jurisdiction of the federal defence ministry. And the weapons which were provided for those purposes were in the warehouses of the Army of Yugoslavia, and that's where the connection could be made between the army and the civilian defence, but actually the weapons were just being stored there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And the army released them, 47.000 of them?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 47.000 or some other number, it's possible. I don't know that specifically, but probably some of the more competent witnesses could explain this. It's possible that other units were also armed from the reserve composition which were under the jurisdiction of the 3rd Army command. But probably a witness can speak about this that is more competent to testify about that. This part I know for sure, the part that is under the jurisdiction of the defence ministry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic, that completes your evidence here; thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it. You are now free to leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, I know it's only ten minutes, but it would be convenient to us if you were to start the witness now and still have the break at 4.00. So who is the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, our next witness is General Simic. Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- I don't know if it's convenient -- oh, but the witness has already been called. I thought perhaps that I could have five minutes relating to some procedural questions that need to be dealt with in private session because the documents that I wanted to discuss were subject to protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Haider will just keep the witness at the door then if you want to do that, and we'll go into private session to hear you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Visnjic, for explaining the complications in relation to the exhibits to which you've referred, and we note the action you propose to take. We shall now have the break and shall resume at 4.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: --- Upon resuming at 4.30 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document now before you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, you will now be examined by Mr. Visnjic on behalf of Mr. Ojdanic. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, General. For the record, can you please tell us your name.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: Miodrag Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, you are retired?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, from the 31st of December, 2001. I retired from the duty of 1st Army commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Which rank did you retire on?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant-general.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General Simic, you told an investigator of the General Ojdanic Defence team, and you gave them a statement which you signed?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Before you testified, did you sign this statement?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And before you came to testify, do you think that there's anything in this statement that you would like to correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: If you were to testify now, would you still give the same answers to the same questions as in the statement?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this statement has been tendered as 3D1089.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, I'm not going to ask you about what you said in the statement. I would just like you to explain some things in more detail and I would like to deal with some facts that are not in your statement. Please, can you tell me when you came to the Supreme Command Staff?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: I came to the Supreme Command Staff on the 2nd of April, 1999, that's when I took up my duties. I occupied or took up the command post at 1500 hours on the 4th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And you were performing which duty before you came to the staff?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: Before I came to the staff, I was the assistant defence minister for sector chief for civilian defence of the MOD. I took over my duty from General Geza Farkas.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And which duty did you assume?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: I assumed the duty of deputy Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command Staff for the land forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement you described in detail what your duties involved in the Supreme Command Staff, so I don't need to go into that again. I would just like to ask you about your first appearance at the evening briefing - and this is 3D724.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be put on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, you attended these briefings regularly with the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command Staff?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, if I was not absent.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at the bottom of the page in B/C/S, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, we have your contribution to this evening briefing of the 6th of April. Can you please tell me, what did the 3rd Army commander's proposal relate to and how was this proposal resolved?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, it's a little bit larger now because I don't have the correct glasses. Can you please just tell me the question and the place again?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Can you look at the last item here which says: "Proposal of the command -- commander."

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: Besides reporting on the situation in the theatre of war to the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command Staff, we were also duty-bound to report on the requests of the commander to the Supreme Command Staff, and in the spirit of that, to suggest to the chief a way to resolve a particular request. Here it was requested that students of the fourth year of the military academy and of the high school be -- that their schooling be curtailed and that they be sent to the units of the Pristina Corps, which was then replenished 87.7 per cent with officers and 87.8 per cent with non-commissioned officers. They were lacking 1.116 --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Can you just go a little bit slower. I know that you are very thorough in your explanations, but can you be a little bit slower for the sake of interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: So they were lacking 1.116 officers and 836 non-commissioned officers. These were all key posts that involved direct combat duties. These were platoon and company commanders, and that is why he asked the replenishment to be done in this way. In accordance with the request of the Chief of Staff, I proposed that this request or proposal is not accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us why?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: The final-year students are not capable of performing such responsible tasks during wartime, and it would be the personal -- their personal sacrifice. It would be sacrificing their lives and not only just their lives, but the lives of the members of the units that they commanded because they were not adequately trained to command in combat situations.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, still later you found a way to implement this request by the chief of the 3rd Army, you found a different, more favourable way?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, a more favourable way was found, but these units were never 100 per cent replenished in terms of these particular posts.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This report, can we look at page 4 in B/C/S, please, and page 4 in English also?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Can we have the same size of letters both in the B/C/S and in the English so that I could use the same pair of glasses for both.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we zoom in on paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, you need be concerned --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You need be concerned with only the B/C/S version, and Mr. Visnjic will ensure, I hope, as will those controlling the technology, that it's clear enough for you to read.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, in this text in paragraph 3 at the end there are the tasks issued by the Chief of the General Staff. A map is mentioned. Can you explain to us what this map is, and you were issued an assignment here, you and General Cucin.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: The command posts from the battalion commanders upwards up to the Supreme Command Staff, there was a working map. In this case this was a working map of the Supreme Command Staff chief where all of their activities in a 24-hour period are shown. After certain amount of time, if you're thinking of this assignment specifically, the Chief of Staff noticed that it was not really that legible, and I was given the assignment, together with General Cucin as the operations administration person to find a way and to suggest how to keep the working map in a way that it would be very clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Let us just explain to the Trial Chamber, but let's not do it in military language. So this is a map --

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: This is a map in the operations room of the centre where all the connections were.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Thank you. I'm going to lead you now. So this is a map which is on the wall --

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: It's on the wall in the operations centre --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, what the size of this map is more or less?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember the size of the map. It was perhaps 1.5 by 1.5.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And what is entered into this map?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: The map is -- features the units in their engagements, also in the war diary all their activities are registered. And then if there was a movement of a specific unit, this is indicated in a special colour, and then in the legend this -- it's explained which period this refers to. And this is the working map of the Supreme Command Staff for the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you now tell me, all the strategic groups were entered into the map, I'm thinking of the land army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And which particulars were registered on the map in relation to the strategic groups, which units were shown on the map?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: According to our rules, the working map would include units that are two levels down. In this case these would be the corps and their dis -- disposition or deployment. We made an exception for the Pristina Corps, and we also showed that as part of the corps or brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now please have the following document, 3D639. This is the briefing for the next day. Your Honours, I think there is a problem. This document, there has been some confusion when the document was logged. I'll just go with General Simic through three lines of this document, and then there will be a translation at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, I've been warned about page 50, line 9. Let me ask you again about the Pristina Corps. You said that the units, too, were registered, not just the corps?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, and the brigades, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And the brigades, too, all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
