utterances.text: [Interpretation] 3D639. This is the briefing that took place on the next day, the 7th of April. Could we please show page 1 of that document in B/C/S, the bottom of page 1. Bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, if you look at paragraph 4 we see your contribution there again. The second line says that the working map was already produced, it was the one that you were talking about a while ago?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, we made this proposal to the chief of the Supreme Command. He raised certain objections and made certain suggestions. He sent us back to the drawing board, in a manner of speaking, so the next day we drew up the final version, and he was perfectly happy with that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Based on what did you enter information into this working map?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: Information centered into the working map based on combat reports from subordinate units.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Can you now comment on the first bullet or line in your contribution.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the English is entirely erroneous. This is not even the same document. Therefore, I think it would be a good idea for us to use the Serbian version alone. Could we please scroll down to the very bottom of this page in Serbian. The same document, thank you --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, that is presenting a problem for me not having the English. Also this exhibit and the last one, I have an authenticity objection to because there's no stamp, there's no signature, there's no way to know when this document was created or by whom, and we haven't had any evidence from this witness other than commenting on what appears to be his contribution in these notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, Mr. Stamp cross-examined the last witness by reference to a number of briefing notes. Are these ones exceptional or do they all follow the same form?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know. I didn't -- I didn't look at the ones that Mr. Stamp was dealing with. I just know that at least two or three with this witness are in that same form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you should alert us to those which you object to, and we note D724 and D639 are objected to --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Also 3D725, I have an objection to because there's no signature. I don't think it's the same form as this, and that's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Visnjic, you're alerted to the possibility of some contention over authenticity, and meanwhile you should proceed and we will deal with that in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Sir, General. You see this first line, right, where you refer to a possible incident at Vinca, can you explain what this is about, please, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you please scroll down. I'm talking about Mr. Simic's contribution paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Bearing in mind the operations that had been conducted by the aggressor up to that point, they had been destroying both the civilian and the military infrastructures, the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command expressed his concern as to what would happen should there be any destruction of the Vinca institute, and that is why he ordered me to enlist the assistance of my ABHO assistant to go there to investigate the situation on the spot and to propose measures for that eventuality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, the authenticity of the English version is a matter in your control. You're the person who uploads this material, and we note that this is not the English version relevant to 3D639 but require you, if possible, by tomorrow to get this rectified so that it can be dealt with properly in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I had brought this to the attention of the Defence team before today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Rather, Your Honours, there's something I must say, we have a problem with the CLSS because they returned this translation. I hope we can go back to them, talk to them, and track this down tomorrow morning at best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, my impression is that you should already have that in train --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, page 52, line 23, what do you mean by assistant for ABHO or NBC, nuclear, biological, and chemical warfare?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: He's not an assistant, he's the chief for the NBC administration, the nuclear, biological, and chemical warfare protection. He is one of my subordinates. I had five administrations under me that were headed by generals.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And what is this facility at Vinca?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: It's a well-known nuclear institute, and there is a lot of radio-active matter being stored there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we turn the page, please, go to the next page. Top of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, can you comment on what we see in the first two lines. There's a reference to the engineering units at the Sava and Danube and volunteers as well.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I can't see that myself. I can't see it on the screen, what you're asking me about.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: You should be able to see that, shouldn't you, it's at the top of the page. You see what it says toured the chief of the engineering units --

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I see that it was the established practice for the administration heads to tour their units on a daily basis in the Belgrade area and very often elsewhere. They would just go off on their own accord to tour units in Kosovo as well, for example. There was a danger, not just a danger, some bridges had actually an destroyed. I sent the engineering chief to see what the combat-readiness of the units at the Sava and the Danube was, I'm talking about the engineering units, bearing in mind the possibility to establish ferry crossings.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: There is a reference to training 126 volunteers, General. What's that about?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: Some volunteers reported and expressed their wish to be involved in the country's defence. The Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command saw it fit, regardless of their patriotic sentiment and their duties, that we should train these people in our training centres. One such centre was at Bubanj Potok. Once their training was done, they were sent to Kosovo and Metohija to join the Pristina Corps, be in the area covered by the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's move on to our next exhibit, please, P929, page 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, this is a collegium meeting dated the 9th of April, 1999?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Based on your memory, why was this meeting particularly important?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: I told you already that we had daily briefings in the evening at which the daily situation all along the front line was analysed, and the Chief of Staff would hand out assignments. After some time, it's D plus 17, if I remember well, it was after 17 days of war, there was a generally held belief that it was necessary to conduct a thorough analysis of how the country had been defended up to that point. It was necessary to review the results of the aggression, and it was necessary to see what could be done in terms of adjusting the operative deployment of units.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: In this document, on page 13 more specifically, that's the B/C/S reference. The English reference is page 12, the bottom of the page as well, you report to the Chief of the General Staff, and I will read you the last three lines. They read: "Based on the decision of the commander of the 3rd Army, the operative deployment of units was done in Kosovo and Metohija. These same units are now involved in protecting the state border, crushing the terrorist Siptar forces, and blocking their axes from the Republic of Albania and Macedonia, along which they are conducting operations into the territory of Kosovo and Metohija." Let me ask you a question based on this, sir. Operative deployment of the units, General, based on what sort of documents was this done?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: I apologise. The operative deployment of units was done based on the directive on the use of armed forces for defending the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: What are initial operative plans, General?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: Initial operative plans are plans that are designed at the operation -- by the operations administration of the General Staff. This is normally done in peacetime. A threat to the country's security is envisaged and the plan is based on this. This may never materialise, but if it does the situation is monitored and then the plan is adjusted.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: In this specific case, the 9th of April, 1999, the war has now been going on for nearly 15 days. What was the idea behind the deployment of VJ units in Kosovo and Metohija in this particular case?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: The operative deployment of units in Kosovo and Metohija basically was done based on a directive called Thunder 3, Grom 3, which was passed by the General Staff on the 16th of January.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have that same document placed on e-court, please, page 15 in the B/C/S and page 14 in the English. Your Honours, in order to save time I will not be quoting much from this document, but let me refer you to page -- pages 12 through 15 in English where General Simic's contribution is reproduced in detail about the intentions of the VJ at the time. The lower half of the page. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, you see this paragraph that begins: "Up to now, the enemy had not used their air power to any significant extent ..."

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: All right. We see you there providing an assessment about a possible attack by NATO's land forces. Can you provide more detail about that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: If you go through this entire thing, I also pointed out that the ground forces up to that point in time had not suffered any substantial losses, which didn't necessarily mean that the losses that had been sustained can be underestimated. It's always a loss of human lives, isn't it. There were many reasons for this, the first being that initially the aggressor tried to destroy the civilian/military infrastructures in order to prevent any manoeuvres by the VJ along the front line and deep into the territory. Another objective was to destroy key facilities and communications buildings in the VJ structure in order to destroy the command system. At a later stage they would start inflicting substantial losses on manpower itself in the defence sectors. Up to this point in time they had not been successful in achieving this objective. It was based on this that I reckoned that they would not start inflicting losses over the next 10 to 15 days against our manpower, which made the situation favourable for us in terms of continuing to fortify -- to build fortifications, to reinforce, to try to improve on some of our weaknesses in terms of discipline and such-like. And that was the context in which I used this expression.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, I asked you about the basic idea, and you said the basic idea for defence, you said this idea stemmed from some elements of the plan that was known as Thunder 3 or Thunder-bolt 3?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Initially during the early stage of the aggression when the attack first occurred, was there a change in the assignment given to units?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: If you will allow me, I would just like to say in Thunder 3 it was our assessment that the aggression would be launched simultaneously from the air and with the air-borne assaults by a multi-national brigade, and this is why we tasked some of our units with being ready to block and destroy those air-borne units. Because the aggression was not launched in this manner, it was considered that because air-borne assaults could no longer be performed, that we should improve our operative disposition, issue new taks and to prepare for the ground attack that we expected, and this was something that the Supreme Command Staff always expected.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Let us not go into details now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you clarify for me what you mean when you say: "Because the aggression was not launched in this manner, it was considered that because air-borne assaults could no longer be performed, that we should improve our operative decision ..."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I don't want to make any doubts about the interpretation. I didn't say that no air-borne assault would be carried out. In our Grom 3 directive, we assessed that the aggression would be launched by simultaneous air-borne assaults by a multi-national brigade in Kosovo and air-strikes, because we thought that they would then link-up with the ground forces. After 17 days of war, we realised that no air-borne assault had taken place and that is why I explained this in this manner. I didn't say that there would be no air-strikes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is an air-borne assault then, because my understanding is that there was bombing over these 17 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think we're talking about air-borne assaults.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, if you allow me, I can explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Air-strikes are defined as attacks from the air using all assets available, and at the beginning I indicated that the enemy wanted to prevent our units from manoeuvring and to destroy our chain of command, our commanding system, by attacking civilian and military infrastructure. I said that we expected the enemy to continue doing that even after this period in order to disable the infrastructure and the command system and then to carry out strikes. But in Grom 3 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But what do you mean by an air-borne assault? Is that the flying-in of personnel rather than the flying-in of weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I say "air-strikes," I mean attacks launched by the aircraft and cruising missiles -- cruise missiles on all the infrastructure. Air-borne assaults, that refers partly to operations from the air-space and bringing in of ground forces by land.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you -- well, when you say -- I'm still not understanding you. Why would you call bringing in troops by land an air-borne assault?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't say bringing the troops in by land was part of an air-strike. The air-borne assaults, that's bringing in the troops by air, and those troops can maintain -- hold an area for a certain point -- period of time. But if you don't have a ground attack, if you don't bring in ground troops by land, they cannot hold on to that piece of territory that they had taken in an air-borne assault. That's what happened to Russians, they lost an entire battalion in a very short period of time in the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: In Afghanistan.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I hope that you understand it from the interpretation. It's still not clear to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand it now it thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, fine. Let us go back to this possibility that a ground operation could be launched. At one point several options were under consideration regarding this ground attack. Could you please tell us something more about that.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: I've already said that at the Supreme Command Staff there was always this concern or this assessment that sooner or later there would be a ground operation, provided that the air-strikes achieved the objectives that I outlined in my previous answers. Now, as for the modalities of the ground operation, there were several options there. If you need me to do so, I can explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Could you please explain to us some of the modalities that you believed might actually occur and what needed to be done on our side, or rather, what forces should have been brought to what positions in order to counter some of those modalities, to stop them, but please go slow. Everybody's tired and it's very important for this to be conveyed properly.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: We thought that there were two options for a ground operation. Option one is that by involving the terrorist army in Kosovo with the support from the Albanian army, a large bridge might be set up and which could later involve NATO forces, too. Option two, a smaller-scale operation, was for NATO ground forces to do so right away. Why did I say that this was -- that this was not so -- that was not as likely as the first one, it's because we figured that NATO was not so likely to sacrifice its soldiers, and that's why we thought that they would use the terrorists and the people from Albania to set up the bridge head. And the bridge head is -- and the term "bridge head" is for us soldiers a piece of territory, maybe 5 or 10 kilometres away from the Albanian border, in the depth of the Kosovo territory which would be sufficient for NATO to get in with its troops and then to expand this territory, finally gaining the whole of territory -- the control of the whole of territory of Kosovo without suffering any losses by linking up with the terrorist forces in the Kosovo territory, thereby carrying out its task.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, this was the minutes from the collegium where you made your presentation on the 9th of April, but on the 9th of April the General Staff issued yet another document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that's document P1481, but I don't want it to be brought up on e-court. I would like 4D107 to be brought up, it is the same document, in fact. The problem with P1481 lies in the fact that only the first page in B/C/S has actually been uploaded into the system.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, you are familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us, what is this document?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: It's a directive.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: What is a directive in the hierarchy of military documents?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: Only the Supreme Command Staff can issue directives. It's the highest type of order that decides how the Army of Yugoslavia is to be deployed in the whole theatre of war over a longer period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown -- well, in this specific case, this is the directive.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Could you please give us its exact title?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: "Directive for the engagement of the Yugoslavia Army in the defence against the NATO aggression."

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please look at page 5 in B/C/S and page 5 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, we have in front of us paragraph 2 which is entitled: "The concept and the idea of strategic defence." Could you please explain to the Judges those two terms, "concept" and "idea," as used in military parlance.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: Before giving you this specific answer, can I just say one sentence. All of our documents are quite formalised, quite formal, and the directive is not an exception. So you can always -- you always have the same chapters there, enemy, and so on. So "concept" and "idea," it is an integral part of such a document, it is the concept of the Supreme Command in which it decides how it will lead its army in the defence of the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Let me rephrase it in simple terms. This is the concept about how a war is to be waged, how a country is to be defended?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, you could put it that way too.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please ...

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Could you please comment on this text that you see in front of you, and to explain to us what was the concept of the Army of Yugoslavia, or rather, the General Staff when this document was made.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: In the first paragraph in the preamble of the second paragraph it is stated that "The engagement and the use of" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down when reading.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That "The engagement and the use of the Army of Yugoslavia in the defence against the NATO should be carried out in two stages with the full application of the provisions of the Geneva Conventions and international law of war and humanitarian law."

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I know -- I know that this may be difficult for you, but you don't have to read slower, you just have to make pauses after you complete a sentence.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I will do that. When I said that those documents always follow the same format, I want to note that there was no need for this provision "with full application of the provisions of the Geneva Conventions" and so on to be included here, because there is a place for that word -- for those words to be included, and that's not the place. But at the insistence of the chief of the Supreme Command Staff, he wanted that to be included. And that was the first time in my military career that I was faced with the situation in which in an essential part of a document of this sort, this wording was included. By doing that, he wanted all of his subordinates to become aware of the seriousness of this demand as to how they should conduct themselves when carrying out the tasks that they received in the defence of the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, could you please look at stage 2, paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we just scroll down a little bit the B/C/S version of the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Second stage, first phase. Could you please comment on this phase and that was anticipated in the -- in the concept.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: We knew that in the defence of the country so far, the Siptar, or rather, the terrorist army of Kosovo had not been destroyed. It had been routed, it was not a danger as a unified organisation. Some of its elements had managed to pull out to the territory of Albania in order to save themselves in the face of destruction. And we considered that at a propitious moment in their assessment they would return to the territory of Kosovo by one way or another. We also knew that some of the ethnic Albanians, for one reason or another - I could discuss them if required to do so by the honourable Trial Chamber - had fled to Albania and that at one point in time they would be coming back one way or another.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, was there any concept of the Army of Yugoslavia or any other document where the idea was elaborated to the effect that the population should be expelled across the border in order to improve the ethnic composition in Kosovo, the ethnic balance in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: I did not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of any VJ document or any meeting, briefing, or any informal discussions where the idea was mooted that the population should be expelled in order to improve the ethnic balance in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, a brief reply would be no, but if you allow me to elaborate --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: No, a brief answer would suffice. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: But could I please comment on this? I would like to be allowed to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: Had there been such a plan, had we done that, the chief of the Supreme Command Staff would not have ordered his subordinates how to treat the refugees should they appear at the border. He is warning them there, he is ordering them even, to cooperate with the authorities in taking care of these people. And if terrorist forces are being infiltrated under the guise of returning refugees, that should be prevented. So you can see that the chief of the Supreme Command Staff is ordering his commanders how to act. Had any such plan been in existence, the chief of the Supreme Command Staff would not have issued an order of this nature to his subordinates.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. You said the Chief of Staff issues orders to his subordinates. How could the Supreme Command Staff chief implement this responsibility in practice? How did he have insight into what was happening - in this case specifically on the territory of Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: Everything is regulated in our rules. The Supreme Command Staff chief had several channels through which he could learn - and he did learn about the situation on the front. One of the important ones was direct telephone contact with commanders using a protected line; a second way was a combat report that arrived daily from subordinate commands; the third was personal presence or sending the most responsible officers for inspection to see in the field what the situation was; and finally, via intelligence and counter-intelligence organs, he could also find out what the situation in the field was.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like to ask you something about this control you mentioned, control or inspection. Can you tell me what this inspection is. Is it a command function?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: Inspection or control is a process function of command. Others include planning of a certain activity, organising, implementation, control, and analysis at the end. These are the process command functions. Control or inspection is very important in that chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, do you know how the control function was organised during the war? Who carried out this function and how frequently was it done?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: The control function is organised by sending specific organs from the Supreme Command Staff who would see for themselves by spending a certain amount of time at the control facility, see what the combat-readiness of the units was, or rather, in one sentence, they would see if the unit was carrying out its assignments in the spirit of the orders received, if there was any deviation or problem in that, and what the manner of their resolution was. Besides sending senior officers, the Supreme Command Staff - let me say this as well - there was also an inspection of the Army of Yugoslavia, headed at that time by General Samardzic, which also performed this control duty. It also went into the field to control subordinate units, or rather, not control but inspection.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: So we have control and inspection?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And now, can you please tell me if you ever went to this control on the territory of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: When I assumed the duty at the Supreme Command Staff, I went to this control job three times. Once I headed a team, once I was a deputy head of the team, and one time I was head of control at the facility that was being controlled.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: When you went to this control task, can you please describe to the Chamber what is done when you come to the unit or what you call the control facility.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: The facility that is controlled is at the rank of a brigade. When you come to the unit, the Supreme Command Staff - and it was explicit in this in view of the risk undertaken in the journey - he ordered that one or two days would be spent to go or to come back using only daylight, and then at the control facility two days had to be spent continuously for a period of 24 hours in the work and life conditions that prevailed for the soldiers and the senior officers of the facility that was undergoing control. This means that if there was a dug-out, the person would have to be in a dug-out; if they were in a tent, the person would be in a tent; if they were in a building, they would have to be in a building.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us generally what you established? Just one moment, please, what you established in these controls and later we will then deal with this one particular control for which we have documents.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: These three controls that I conducted, in general we established that units essentially were carrying out assignments in the spirit of orders received with minor deviations which did not significantly influence the execution of the assignments. And if measures were not taken to alleviate these deviations, they could put in question the further execution of a particular assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please look at 3D693. Your Honours, we are going to see in a minute an order of the Supreme Command Staff about control specifically in the way that General Simic explained it to us. I would like to look at paragraph 2.2. Can we zoom in on that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, this item 2.2 -- actually, what is contained in that paragraph, 2.2?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: In item 2.2, evidently we can see that it's an assignment set by the Supreme Command Staff about what we needed to look at in the units subject to control, but I have to say, you said that it was a control. I didn't see the date here, but I think it's from the 22nd until the 26th. If I remember correctly, and this control was conducted in the Pristina Corps and for other units at the regiment brigade level. I can see the date here, it's from the 23rd to the 26th - I apologise - at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at page 3 of this document. Can we look at the middle part of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, I see here that you were in charge of control of the Pristina Corps command; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: Partially, yes. You can see here that general -- the late Colonel -- Lieutenant-General Ljubisa Velickovic was the head of the unit controlling the Pristina Corps. I was his deputy, and together with him controlled just the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at 3D692.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, soon we're going to see a report. Can you please tell us now what this document is, how it came to be, and what was the procedure after the control was carried out.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: I must say that the control itself implied several documents, the initial document, the order, then the next document, the report, and then at the end the order of the superior - in this case the Supreme Command Staff chief - to resolve the problems noted. In this case, this is a written report submitted by the team leader to the Supreme Command Staff chief on the 29th of May, as was ordered in the order. But if you permit me --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Just one moment, please. Go ahead, General.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: I must say that each team - this was the usual practice - was obliged to state its preliminary findings to the most responsible officer in the field so that the Pristina Corps command the same day that we completed the control was informed about the situation that we found to avoid the situation of informing them about one situation and reporting on it differently.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: So after two or three days in the field, you would practically report your findings to the unit being controlled, and upon return, in this case to the General Staff, you would draft the report which you would send to the General Staff chief?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: On the 26th in the morning we reported to the corps commander our findings, and on the same day we left for Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you explain why these -- the order was given in relation to the 2nd Army and the Pristina Corps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Supreme Command Staff chief would decide where he would send his people, his subordinates, to carry out controls. This control in the Pristina Corps, the one that we're speaking about now, also had a particular problem because on the 17th or the 18th, if I remember correctly, there was a considerable degree of desertions, I would not term it mass desertion, but significant numbers left their positions, and I'm thinking of a part in the 354th brigade --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch all the units.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and he wanted to see what the situation was in as short time as possible. The 2nd Brigade [as interpreted] was not so good in relation to the call-up response, and he decided with his deputy to send someone to look at what the situation was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So this didn't occur because there was some marriage between the activities of the Pristina Corps and the 2nd Army; it's coincidence, is it, that they're both referred to in the same order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understood the question properly, these were not married cases, but the directive does speak about acting in coordination. But the problem of desertion in these units was pronounced as well as insufficient response to call-up in the navy. But there was nothing else in terms of coordinated action with these units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, page 71, line 16, it should say the 2nd Army instead of the 2nd Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And I have just been told, General, can you please repeat which brigades had a problem in the Pristina Corps. You mentioned some of them, but it was not recorded in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: These were characteristics, the 7th Infantry Brigade from Krusevac; a battalion of the 125th Motorised Brigade from Kosovska Mitrovica; and from what I can remember, I'm not sure, I think it was a part of -- smaller part of a unit from the 354th Infantry Brigade from Kursumlija.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, this document was logged in on the 29th of May, 1999?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. If you are thinking about the report about the executed control.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes. And on the 26th you completed the control; on the 27th you were on the trip back. What happened from the 26th to the 29th?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, a small correction. I said that on the 26th we reported to the Pristina Corps commander about the situation found, and on the same day in the evening we arrived at Belgrade. Upon our arrival to Belgrade, the team chief and myself as his deputy orally reported the same as we reported to the corps commander at his command post. From the 26th in the evening until the set deadline on the 29th, we processed the report, in the technical sense, and we submitted it to the Supreme Command Staff chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: On page 5 and 6 in B/C/S, and it's the same pages in the English, you made a set of -- you proposed a set of measures in order to correct the weaknesses. Is that the usual procedure upon completion of the control --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you answer that, can I advise you that the interpreters are having some difficulty keeping up with your pace of speech. So could you try to speak more slowly so that we get the whole context of what you're saying. There's the odd bit that may have been missed as a result of speed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, thank you. I will try to give briefer answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, it would be sufficient if you were slower.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, all right. I accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: So the measures proposed on pages 5 and 6 in the English, also pages 5 and 6 in the B/C/S, is that the information that General Velickovic conveyed to the Supreme Command Staff or to the Supreme Command Staff chief?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we prepare the next document, please, and that is 3D694.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It might be best if you postpone your question on that until we return, or is this the last in a series of questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think this is a convenient time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, this is a time at which we must have a break for 20 minutes, so could you please leave the courtroom with the usher. And we'll see you again at five minutes past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [The witness takes the stand].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see the situation has improved. I hope the sound will be a little slower, too, so the interpreters can follow.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: Thank you, and I would certainly like to thank the President of the Chamber for his offer for me to get a new pair of glasses. I'm still intellectually fit, it was just the wrong set of glasses. I actually own both sets, but I got the wrong one, and now I have both so it's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We'll find the mistranslation somewhere later.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We were looking at 3D692 before the break. This was a control report dated the 29th of May, 1999. If I may just remind the Chamber - and I move this document be looked at in its entirety - pages 5 and 6 contain proposed measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: All right, General. You inform us that the team leader, General Velickovic informed the Chief of the General Staff about this control.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please look at Exhibit 3D694. This is a one-page document and the title is: "Dealing with shortcomings that had been noticed," and this is an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, can you please look at paragraph 3 of this document and can you please explain what is being ordered here by the Chief of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: This document clearly shows that the Chief of the General Staff of the Supreme Command entirely accepted reports of the team leader, and in particular the measures proposed for dealing with any weaknesses that were noted. In order to curtail the time needed for this correspondence to take place between the army staff and the -- army command and the supreme staff, he didn't see it fit that these measures, same measures, should be made operational according to this same system and drafted as a separate order. He therefore restricted himself to briefly ordering for this proposal to be transformed into an order that he would then sign.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, could you please now look at 3D700. This is a 3rd Army document. What is it exactly, General?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: One can see here that the 3rd Army command received the order of the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command and its own Chief of Staff signed this, General Stojmirovic. He is sending to one of his subordinate commands, in this case the command of the Pristina Corps, instructions to start eliminating any weaknesses that were noted. This is something that was attached to another document. It says that the elimination plan is enclosed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, who was this document sent to?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: This document was sent to the Supreme Command Staff. I may have misspoken a while ago because I was only relying on the wording and I didn't look up at the header, but in the order we ordered for them to draw up a plan to deal with any weaknesses and shortcomings. A copy of that plan was to be forwarded to the Supreme Command Staff by them, and this is the very document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you now please look at the next document -- rather, my apologies. As for this plan, General, pages 2 through 4, what we see listed there are measures to be taken, and they are divided according to particular topics in terms of combat-readiness, elements of combat-readiness. Can you explain this diagram that we see before us for the benefit of the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, you're spending an awful lot of time on events at the end of May and the beginning of June. Do you really need to spend your very valuable oral evidence time on this sort of thing rather than give it to us to read for ourselves?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this document is for me an example of the work and competences of General Ojdanic. I'm using it in the sense of functioning, and I want to show what it was that General Ojdanic did, what was within his purview and within his competences. I think the events addressed by this topic do not touch on the very heart of the matter that we are about to deal with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, I wonder if there aren't similar documents in the period between December and April that would be more directly relevant to the issues in the indictment. Still, I don't want to take up even more of your valuable time. Please continue as quickly as you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, measures are divided by their respective topics, right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: No, they're divided in terms of elements of combat-readiness. In this specific case we're talking about command as the first principal element of combat-readiness. There is command, there is preparedness and level of training, mobilisation readiness, morale and information, logistics, and logistics security.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And finally, 3D701.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, what is this document?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: A plan to eliminate weaknesses observed during a visit to the Pristina Corps units by the Supreme Command Staff. It was sent to the Pristina Corps command. May I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, by all means.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: What this means is this. The army command informed us what they had done in terms of our order, and then they ordered their subordinate command, the Pristina Corps command, certain measures that they were to take.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: All right, General. For the last one and a half hours, or nearly, you've been telling us about the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command. Who are you actually talking about? Who was this?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: My apologies. I wasn't cautioned explicitly whether I should use title and rank or whether I should name people; therefore, I decided to go for title and rank in terms of name it was General Ojdanic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this completes my examination of this witness. I have no further questions and could I please be given credit for interpretation in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Visnjic. Any Defence cross-examination? Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good evening, General.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: Good evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: My name is John Ackerman. I'm the attorney for General Pavkovic, and I have a few questions I'd like to ask you. And basically we're going to look at a few documents so that you can explain them, at least to some extent, to this honourable Trial Chamber. I want to ask you first: Do you remember approximately when it was that clashes began to occur between the 3rd Army, Pristina Corps, and the KLA? In point of time, when did those things first start happening?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: If you're asking me about the specific date, then I can't say. Generally in terms of the time-line, this is May and later, May, June, July, that's when this became particularly prominent, and this was going on in the border belt.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That would have been 1998?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. You asked me about 1998, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Who would have been -- who would have been responsible at that point for engaging the VJ in those skirmishes and authorising the engagement in those skirmishes at the border?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: I, for one, find this to be an ambiguous question. Do you mean who was authorised to authorise the use of the VJ in the border belt or elsewhere? Well, that's one question. If you mean just the border belt, in the border belt there were border units, they had certain powers under the rules governing the work of the border service, and they had the power to stop any attempts at illegal crossing. It wasn't required for anyone to issue them specific tasks or to authorise their use.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that same thing would have been true if the VJ had been attacked, they didn't need an order to allow them to respond to an attack. They had full authority to respond to an attack at any time, correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: Our rules of service which take fourth place in relation to the laws - and I mean the constitution, the Law on Defence, the Law on the Army, and then come the rules of service - and these rules state unambiguously, unequivocally, that any unit under attack must use any means available to protect itself, its manpower, its equipment, or any facility that it might be securing. I apologise, I talked about this being implicit, but it wasn't implicit. It was couched in entirely explicit terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I'd like you to look now at a document, it's 4D377, and it will appear on your screen here in a moment we hope. And what I'm interested in is, once you see what the nature of that document is, is paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: For some reason this document can't be accessed, Mr. Ackerman. Do you have a hard copy of it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, yes, I do, actually. I'm baffled by why it can't be accessed. I have a B/C/S version we can give to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Does he have an English version for us or for Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is there also an English version, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There is. I guess we could put it on the ELMO. Your Honour, I'm very sorry about this. That document has been in e-court for a long time. I don't know why --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the usher will collect the English copy from you, and then put it on the ELMO and give the witness the B/C/S copy in his hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's paragraph 4 we need to see -- no, you'll need to come out a bit. That's it. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Now, Mr. Witness, if you'll look at paragraph 4 of the B/C/S version you have in front of you, what you have there is an order from General Samardzic, and it's dated 29 May of 1998 to the Pristina Corps command. And in that paragraph 4 he seems to order a number of things and it's a bit -- it's a bit vague for those of us that were not part of that organisation. Can you just explain what is meant by paragraph 4. What is it that the recipient of that order is supposed to do?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: Based on the paragraph mentioned, one can see that the army commander orders to his subordinate, the corps commander, to support the MUP forces in carrying out their combat operations by using combat equipment in keeping with their current features. Support is to be provided only at the request of the overall MUP commander and following approval by the commander of the 3rd Army and the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're trying to figure out what's going on, and we just got a message that there has been an access problem with e-court going on all day. So this could get quite tedious if we continue to have a problem, and I don't know quite how to deal with it. I don't have one copy of each of these documents but we would take three times as long to get through this as it would take me if we could access the documents in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, let's see what happens when you call up another one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: General, we've seen some documents in this case - and I don't happen to have one in front of you right now, and I'm not going to take the time to find one and get it in front of you - that contain a sort of common phrase, saying that the VJ is to be used according to the rules of combat use. Does that have a special meaning "according to the rules of combat use"?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: It has no special meaning except for the fact that he warns that there should be no action that was taken outside of the regulations governing our combat activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. The next document I'm going to ask you to look at if we can is 4D379.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not sure how to address this or whether it's my point to raise it, but I think we were provided a list of the documents that Mr. Ackerman was going to use for cross-examination of this witness, and this one and the previous one aren't on the list I was provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, we've raised this matter before.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's been going like this since fairly early this morning. Mr. Hannis is absolutely correct, they're not on the list. They were supposed to be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't object to him using it, but I just need to have it or I want to have it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's -- from time to time there are going to be blips in this arrangement, and time will be given to anyone who turns out to be prejudiced by a failure that can be excused. And I think in this instance we should deal with it if it does cause actual prejudice. I think Mr. Ackerman realises that it shouldn't have happened, but sometimes these things just can't be avoided. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, let me just very quickly put on the record because it will just take a few seconds to do it, the documents I'm going to use, 4D379, 4D380, 4D183, maybe 4D129, 4D138, 4D297, 4D134, 4D91, 4D378, 4D141, 4D229, 4D375, 3D697, 4D136. Now, what we were trying to get is 4D379, and apparently that one can't be brought up in e-court either. So, Judge, I don't know what you want to do. This is going to take two or three times as long as it would if e-court was working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think the sensible thing is to use the assistance you have beside you to marshal the hard copies so that we can do exactly what we've done with 4D377 and to make allowances in looking at the time. Let's say we'll not charge the next 25 minutes to anyone, Mr. Ackerman, how's that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour, I just hate to waste time like this because it is precious; I understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The document you're seeing now is dated 7 April 1998, and it's an order from General Perisic, commanding general of the VJ. And what I'm interested in is paragraph 2, and can you interpret that for us and tell us what that paragraph means when he says "to relocate part of the RMR from certain places to other places." What is that about?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: In light of the fact that in the Pristina Corps area the situation was deteriorating rapidly, and given that in some sectors we had ammunition depots and depots where other weapons were stored, and it was quite difficult, given the complex situation, to relocate these safely. The Chief of General Staff ordered that these two depots be relocated to safer locations, for the most part outside of the territory of Kosovo or in the north of the province, by that I mean the Leposavic site.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What is RMR?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: That's an acronym for wartime materiel reserves; to be quite specific, those depots contained ammunition and explosives of virtually all calibre.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And do you know where these Bair and Lukare depots were located?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: Bair and Lukare are located in areas which are 100 per cent inhabited by Albanians. In 1981 we had problems when there were some protests and rallies. In the Podujevo area there was the Territorial Defence depot, and there was a danger that those protesters might actually break into the depot and get weapons. This was quite inaccessible, narrow streets, high walls, and it was really quite favourable --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Where are these places that this is being moved to, Kursumlija, Leposavic, and Mirnicka Reka, where are those?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: I've already noted that those depots were relocated to sites in the north of Kosovo, Leposavic, and the other two sites, one is on the Prokuplje-Kursumlija road, and the other one is in the Kursumlija area; that's outside of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And does this indicate an awareness on 9 March of 1988 [sic] on the part of General Perisic as to what specifically was going on in Kosovo at that time?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: I think that it was not the 9th of March. If you're asking me about this document that you showed me, that would be the 7th of April. And to be quite specific and to answer your question, my answer would be yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, it's been drawn to my attention that the problem here with the documents is caused by the failure to release them into the court's e-court system and that that's now being done and resolving the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, that was the question I just had asked of my associate, and I was told that that had happened. I have been standing here worried that it hadn't, though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So you can take it that we'll be revoking what we said about the 25 minutes and confine it to the five minutes of confusion. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Let's try to look at 4D380. Now, what you should see in front of you is a 20 April 1998 order from the 3rd Army to the Pristina Corps signed by General Samardzic. And what I'm interested in is the preamble in paragraph 1. Just tell us basically what is it that General Samardzic is ordering by this order.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: The previous document, talking about the relocation of the wartime materiel reserves, prompted me to say that the situation in Kosovo was expected to deteriorate, and this document, in fact, confirms that. It is dated only 13 days later. It confirms that indeed the situation had deteriorated, in particular in the border area, in the areas of the 55th and the 53th Border Battalions. To make it clearer, that would be Djakovica-Decani area. The Chief of General Staff, or rather, the army commander, orders the Pristina Corps commander to take up the forward command post in Djakovica, to set it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And what would be the purpose of that order? Why set up that command post, do you know?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: In accordance with our rules, a forward command post is set up when it is necessary for the commander or his Chief of Staff pursuant to an authorisation by the commander, to be as close as possible to the scene where events are developing in order to be able to take appropriate measures promptly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to another document, 4D183, please. This document is a document of the Pristina Corps command, 16 May 1998, and if we went to the end of it we would see that it is signed by General Pavkovic. The first thing that I want to draw your attention to with regard to this, it talks in the preamble about an inspection of the corps by the Chief of the General Staff of the Yugoslav Army on 14 and 15 May 1998. Does that indicate to you that General Perisic would be conducting an inspection of the corps during that time?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't able to see here on the screen this particular reference that you just made, but the Chief of General Staff did not carry out inspections. We in the General Staff have a special organ authorised to carry out inspections. This officer, or rather, he toured the Pristina Corps in order to see for himself what the combat-readiness status was in the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If we could go to the first page of the B/C/S at the top where the preamble is, then you will be able to see what it is I'm referring to. And it seems to say there that the Chief of the General Staff was going to inspect, doesn't it.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that was General Perisic, was it not?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, you are right. But this was not an inspection but a tour of the unit. I have to note that at the General Staff there is an inspection to determine the combat-readiness of the units of the Army of Yugoslavia, but its composition is quite different than this team that was headed by General Perisic. He led this group of people who went there to visit or tour this unit. If I may clarify, he did not send his inspection. He felt that it would be necessary for he himself to see the situation in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm a bit confused now. I don't know if there's a mistranslation in the document or not. The English document uses the word "inspection," but I don't know if that inspection appears in the first line of the B/C/S version, does it? It doesn't. I'm told that it does not so we have a translation error.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, look at the very first line of the introduction to the document after the address to the commander. Could you read that first line, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, in the preamble it says: "On the basis of the situation observed when the corps units were toured by the Chief of General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia on the 14th and the 15th of May, 1998, problems that were presented by the corps commander and the observations" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's fine. Thank you very much. That deals with the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I want you to look now at paragraph 4 of this document. We've had testimony or evidence in this case before this point, General, where it was suggested that training activities of the VJ in Kosovo were primarily designed to provoke the Albanians into attacking them --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not sure that's a correct statement of the evidence. We talked about one specific training event, but not training in general.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I think that may be true. I know there was a contention in that regard with regard to Podujevo, I believe it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's the one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But in any event, General, with regard to paragraph 4 there, it appears that what is being ordered there is that the local Albanian population is to be contacted and explained -- and there's -- to get an explanation as to why training activities are being conducted in their area. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. The corps commander orders the commands of the combat groups in the area to get in touch personally with the local Siptar population to tell them why the army left the barracks, to tell them that the troops were not there to cause them any harm or anything of the sort, but that they were there to carry out their activities and to warn them that in accordance with our rules, if they should come under an attack, the troops would respond to any attacks using all combat assets at their disposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. Now, what I'd like you to do --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- the Podujevo incident is after the October agreements. This is May 1998. Are you suggesting some connection?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No, none whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I just want to try to explain that these training activities were normal and regular and were done carefully.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'd like you to look at --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Back at that preamble paragraph again, so we could move up just a little bit with the B/C/S so that he can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: After it talks about this tour by the Chief of the General Staff, it talks about problems reported and in order to eradicate failures and weaknesses and improve the general state of combat-readiness, I hereby order ... Now, does that mean that General Pavkovic is basically making an order at the suggestion or even at the order of General Perisic to take care of a few of these things that General Perisic found that maybe were deficient?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: I believe that from the answers I gave Mr. Visnjic, you were able to grasp the methodology for our controls, the controls that we carried out. So this is one such instance of a control where the Chief of General Staff noted there was some weaknesses and ordered that those be eliminated, nothing more than that. And this is nothing out of the ordinary.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Please look at paragraph 8, then, as we scroll down through this document, it's the second page of B/C/S. There it is. In paragraph 8 General Pavkovic talks about operations being undertaken, and he says, They should not involve themselves in unnecessary clashes without the approval of the corps command. They must not impose an exodus or inflict losses on the civilian population. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And then the next paragraph, 9, prohibits Pristina Corps units and combat groups from entering populated areas to search, clear, arrest individuals, bring persons in, or conduct other activities on any basis whatsoever without a special order by the Pristina Corps command, correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, completely.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And finally in paragraph 11 talks about a situation where there might be an attack by -- I guess that's the KLA on Pristina Corps units, and General Pavkovic says that before responding to such an attack, warn the attackers to halt operations and move away from the roads and installations and also call upon the civilian population to move away from that zone. Now, would that have been the civilian population moving away in anticipation that there might be a fight or a battle that could put them in some kind of danger?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, and if you allow me to comment on this whole paragraph, with your permission of course, but if you want a brief answer the answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, if you have something important to say about the paragraph, please do.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: I think that the corps commander in a certain sense sacrificed his own personnel in order to prevent any provocations of his units, because our rules indicate that if you come under attack you should not warn anyone. You just have to defend yourself using all means available. This speaks to the level of responsibility the corps commander evinced for given the complex situation his unit was in.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you this: Where were you during this part of 1998, April, May, up through the Milosevic-Holbrooke Agreement, where were you located?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: If you're asking me for this entire period, I can say that I was in Kosovo and at the army command in Nis I was in Kosovo three times from the 29th of May until the 8th of June. I was at the forward command post of the Pristina Corps and some of the time in Pec, where I was in a different capacity. Then, from the 27th of May until the 28th of August, I was at the forward command post of the 3rd Army in the Pristina barracks, where I set up this forward command post, and I was in charge of it. The third time that I was in the Pristina Corps area was in the first ten days of December 1999 --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think you've gone far enough now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I wonder if we have the exact dates here. You started off by saying that you were in Kosovo three times from the 29th of May until the 8th of June; is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, that's not what I said, it must be a misinterpretation. I said that I went to the Pristina Corps area for just one day, conduct -- carrying out tasks that lasted only one day. I indicated just a three longer periods of time that I spent in Kosovo. The first one is from the 29th of May [as interpreted] until the 8th of June, where -- when I was at the forward command post of the Pristina Corps. The second time I was there was from the 27th of July until the 28th of August --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've now clarified it. There was a mistake in the month, which is now clear. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That would be line 16, Your Honour. That's the one?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And what were your duties at that -- during those periods, June and July of 1998?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: I was the Chief of Staff of the 3rd Army, that was my establishment post, I was also the deputy commander of the army. During my first stay in Kosovo at the forward command post, the army commander tasked me to analyse the situation together with his Chief of Staff, and he authorised me, saying that the corps commander need not go to him for some assistance within the framework of the powers that he conveyed to me. In the second time-period --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think you've answered my question as to what you were doing. And I just have one more question I want to ask you, and then we'll break for the evening. Between the beginning of those clashes along the border until July, the end of July, did you ever have any indication that the Pristina Corps was operating independently, without orders, and without knowledge of the 3rd Army or the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: No, and that's not possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's all I have right now, Your Honour. I think it's time. I'll have more in the morning -- in the afternoon tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Simic, we have to stop there for the evening. We will resume tomorrow at 2.15, when it's necessary for you to return and continue your evidence. Meanwhile, it is important that you should have no discussion with anyone about the evidence in this case. It's a rule that is crucial to the establishment by the Trial Chamber of the truth so far as we are able to establish it in this case. Any interference by anyone with any witness's attempt to give a full, honest account would undermine the interests of justice. So I cannot emphasise enough how important it is that there should be no such communication. So please leave the courtroom now with the usher, and we will see you again tomorrow at 2.15. [The witness stands down].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
